title: Gulshan Devaiah Calls Bollywood's Violence Wave an 'Illusion'
excerpt: The actor argues the dominance of violent blockbusters is "an illusion created by box-office reporting" — and is pivoting from villain roles to the family film Little Thomas, out October 23.
body:
• Gulshan Devaiah says the idea that violence dominates Bollywood is "largely an illusion created by box-office reporting" — diverse genres have always coexisted, as they did in the 1970s and 80s.
  • He argues films shouldn't be measured only by the ₹500 or ₹1000 crore mark but by return on investment, pointing to the surprise success of 12th Fail as proof audiences are unpredictable.
  • The comments come as Devaiah pivots from villain roles (Guns & Gulaabs, Kantara: Chapter 1) to lighter fare: the family film Little Thomas releases theatrically on October 23.
  • Watch for it: Little Thomas, directed by Kaushal Oza and co-starring Rasika Dugal, opens October 23; Devaiah is also preparing a horror project titled Anarth.

Is Bollywood drowning in violence? Gulshan Devaiah doesn't think so — or rather, he thinks you're being sold that story. The actor, known for intense villain turns in Guns & Gulaabs and Kantara: Chapter 1, told Hindustan Times that the narrative of hyper-masculine, violent blockbusters defining Hindi cinema is "largely an illusion created by box-office reporting," in comments highlighted by NDTV.

"Largely an illusion created by box-office reporting."

— Gulshan Devaiah, on the idea that violence dominates Bollywood

The 70s and 80s parallel

Devaiah's argument is historical. Diverse genres have always coexisted in Indian cinema, he says, much as they did in the 1970s and 1980s — when the mass appeal of Amitabh Bachchan's "angry young man" thrived alongside the relatable, middle-class characters of actors like Amol Palekar. The violent blockbuster and the quiet drama were never enemies; they were neighbors. What's changed, in his telling, is the lens: an industry conversation fixated on massive financial returns makes the loudest films look like the only films.

What counts as success

That fixation is Devaiah's second target. A film's success, he argues, should not be measured solely by whether it crosses the ₹500 or ₹1000 crore mark, but by its return on investment. His exhibit A is 12th Fail, the Vidhu Vinod Chopra sleeper that became a career milestone on a modest budget — evidence, he says, that audience tastes are unpredictable and varied, and that smaller, content-driven films keep finding both success and audiences while the trade press looks elsewhere.

He extends the point to the country's socioeconomic diversity: an audience as varied as India's naturally supports a wide range of storytelling, and the industry is not as monolithic as it appears to those who only track the highest-grossing titles.

A career deliberately un-typecast

The timing of the remarks is no accident. Devaiah is in the middle of a conscious pivot away from the negative roles that made him one of streaming's most watchable villains. His upcoming Little Thomas, directed by Kaushal Oza and co-starring Rasika Dugal and Hridansh Parekh, centers on a young boy's desire for a sibling — about as far from Kantara's blood-soaked feuds as it gets. It releases theatrically on October 23.

Devaiah describes the shift not as a master plan but as a conscious adjustment: a desire to avoid being typecast, and to curate a filmography that reflects his own eclectic tastes as a moviegoer. He cites Taare Zameen Par and Mani Ratnam's Anjali — emotional, childhood-centered films — as formative influences, and calls Little Thomas a return to that kind of storytelling. He is even preparing to enter the horror genre, which he has previously avoided, with a project titled Anarth.

Why the debate matters

The "violence wave" conversation has real stakes beyond trade headlines. It shapes what gets greenlit, what diaspora audiences assume Indian cinema has become, and what young actors think they must do to break through. Devaiah's counter — that the audience has always had room for different kinds of stories, and still does — is both a defense of the industry's range and a quiet pitch for his own next chapter. On October 23, the box office gets to weigh in.

items.text: Diverse genres coexisted in the 70s and 80s.
Violent blockbusters and quiet dramas were neighbors, not enemies.
Audience tastes are unpredictable and varied.
